title: Who Is Responsible for an AI Agent?
summary: The EU AI Act assigns accountability to people with 'competence, training and authority'. Most registries record the first two. A lever-by-lever map of who can actually stop an agent.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**"Who is responsible for this agent" is usually answered with a name, and the name is usually the wrong unit to answer with.** A business owner gets named accountable for an agent's outcomes and frequently cannot revoke its access, roll back what it did, or shut it off. That lever sits with someone else.


The EU AI Act already says the quiet part. Article 26(2) requires deployers to assign human oversight to people with "the necessary competence, training and authority", and Article 14(4)(e) says oversight means being able to "interrupt the system through a 'stop' button or a similar procedure". Most ownership records capture competence and training. Authority is the field nobody fills in.


The interesting failure isn't the absence of an owner. It's an owner who is real, named and answerable, and who discovers during an incident that being accountable and being able to act were never the same thing.


We think that mismatch is worse than having no named owner at all. A vacancy prompts someone to ask who is in charge. A name with no mechanism behind it looks like the question has already been answered, so nobody keeps asking.


The fix isn't a longer roster. It's recording, next to every name, which of five specific levers that person holds, and who they call for the ones they don't.
